summary: Defines managed objects that provide an inverted mapping of the interface stack table, which records how network interface layers sit on top of each other. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Network interfaces are stacked in layers, and a management table records which layer sits on top of which. RFC 2864 adds a second, upside-down copy of that table so a manager can quickly ask what runs on top of one interface. The copy cannot be edited and adds no new information.

questions: what is the interface stack table
how to find interfaces above an interface in snmp
subtitle: A read-only upside-down copy of the interface stack table, so a manager can find what runs on top of an interface.

tldr.problem: The ifStackTable is indexed with the higher-layer interface first, so finding which interfaces run on top of a given interface means reading the whole table, which is inefficient on devices with many interfaces.
tldr.mechanism: The IF-INVERTED-STACK-MIB adds ifInvStackTable, which holds the same relationships with the lower-layer ifIndex first and the higher-layer ifIndex second.
tldr.outcome: A management application can read one small slice of the new table to see which interfaces sit above a particular interface. The table holds no new information and is read-only.

today: RFC 2864 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the interface stack table defined in RFC 2863.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2864 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular it describes managed objects that provide an inverted mapping of the interface stack table used for managing network interfaces.

Managed objects are accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). Objects are defined with the Structure of Management Information, and this MIB module is compliant with SMIv2. A SMIv1 version can be produced by translation; the result must be semantically equivalent except where objects are omitted because no translation is possible.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo adds one extra table to the network manager's toolbox. It tells the same story as an existing table, but from the other end.

sections.title: Interface Sub-Layers and the ifStackTable
sections.content:
MIB-II (RFC 1213) defines objects for managing network interfaces through a generic interface definition, the 'interfaces' group, together with the ability to define media-specific extensions. Experience showed the need to distinguish the multiple sub-layers beneath the internetwork-layer. The RFC's example is an interface with PPP running over an HDLC link that uses an RS232-like connector; each sub-layer has its own media-specific MIB module.

The IF-MIB (RFC 2863) meets this need by representing each sub-layer as its own conceptual row in the ifTable. It also defines the ifStackTable, which identifies the higher-layer and lower-layer sub-layers through ifIndex pointers to those rows.

Each row of the ifStackTable represents a relationship in which the higher-layer interface runs on top of the lower-layer interface. The ifStackTable is indexed by the ifIndex values of both interfaces, and the IF-MIB chose to put the higher-layer interface first and the lower-layer second.
sections.plainLanguage: A network interface is built in layers, like a stack. An existing table records which layer sits on top of which, but it is arranged by the upper layer first.

sections.title: The Inverted Table
sections.content:
Because the ifStackTable puts the higher-layer interface first, a management application can read a subset of it to find the interfaces underneath a particular interface. To find the interfaces on top, it has no alternative but to read the whole table, which is very inefficient on a device with many interfaces and many rows.

The new ifInvStackTable holds the same information with the INDEX order reversed: lower-layer interface first, higher-layer interface second. It has exactly the same number of rows as the ifStackTable, but the rows appear in a different order, so reading one slice shows what runs on top of a particular interface.

For every ifIndex value z that identifies an active interface, there are always at least two instantiated rows associated with it. For an interface with no others stacked on top or below, they are ifInvStackStatus.z.0 and ifInvStackStatus.0.z. The table contains exactly the same number of rows as the ifStackTable, but in a different order.
sections.plainLanguage: The new table lists the same relationships in the opposite order. Now a manager can look up one interface and see, in one small read, what runs on top of it.

sections.title: The MIB Objects
sections.content:
The module is IF-INVERTED-STACK-MIB and is registered under mib-2 77. It imports the row status convention and the higher- and lower-layer index objects from the IF-MIB.

The table ifInvStackTable is not accessible on its own; its entries are indexed by ifStackLowerLayer first and ifStackHigherLayer second. The only visible object is ifInvStackStatus, of type RowStatus, with MAX-ACCESS read-only.

An instance of ifInvStackStatus exists for each instance of the ifStackStatus object, and vice versa. If ifStackStatus.H.L exists, then ifInvStackStatus.L.H must also exist, and the two always have the same value. Unlike ifStackStatus, the inverted object is not writable: to change a relationship, an application must modify ifStackStatus.H.L, and the change is then reflected in this table.
sections.plainLanguage: You can only look at the new table, not edit it. To change a relationship you edit the original table, and the new one updates itself.

sections.title: Compliance Requirements
sections.content: The module's compliance statement, ifInvCompliance, covers SNMP entities that provide inverted information on the layering of network interfaces. It makes the group ifInvStackGroup mandatory. For ifInvStackStatus, support is only required for the value active(1). The statement also requires the ifStackGroup2 group from the IF-MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: A device that claims to support this table must show the active relationships and must also keep the original stack table.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in this MIB has a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create. If it is implemented correctly, an intruder cannot alter or create any of its objects through direct SNMP SET operations.

SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment. Even on a secure network there is no control over who may access and GET or SET the objects. The RFC recommends implementers consider the SNMPv3 security features, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575). It is then the responsibility of the customer or user to configure the SNMP entity to give access only to principals with legitimate rights.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody can change this table by sending it a command. But anyone who can look at it should be someone you trust, so configure access carefully.
